Name: K3rabiner Toolboard v2
Description: The K3rabiner Toolboard v2 is a passive wiring breakout PCB designed by MathematicalPotato for the DooKi3 Toolhead v2 on the Annex Engineering K3, and it is also Hula-gantry compatible. It is a 2 oz copper, lead-free PCB, fully assembled with genuine Molex and JST connectors in Canada, with a choice of JST-XH or Microfit 3.0 thermistor port. It carries no MCU, stepper driver or communications bus of its own - it tidies the toolhead wiring back to the mainboard. It is sold as a preorder with about a 60-day lead time.
Verdict Label: K3-only passive breakout; preorder with a long lead time
Cons:
Preorder only, with roughly a 60-day lead after the preorder period closes (Nov 15)
Passive breakout only - no MCU, stepper driver or CAN/USB, so all control still runs back to the mainboard
Only fits the MathematicalPotato Toolhead v2 on an Annex K3, not a general-purpose toolboard
Pros:
2 oz copper PCB with genuine Molex/JST connectors, assembled in Canada
Purpose-built for the MathematicalPotato (DooKi3) Toolhead v2 and the Hula gantry, with a revised outline and connector placement
Thermistor port offered as JST-XH or Microfit 3.0 to suit the builder's harness

Name: EBB SB2209
Description: BigTreeTech's CAN toolhead board designed as a drop-in fit for the Voron StealthBurner. It combines an STM32G0B1 MCU, an onboard TMC2209 extruder driver, an ADXL345 accelerometer for input shaping, and a MAX31865 for PT100/PT1000 sensing, all connected over CAN bus or USB-C. A single XT30 cable carries power and CAN data, replacing the usual bundle of toolhead wires. Price basis: $55.99 regular at BIQU (currently $45.99 on Black Friday sale; the old $46.99 was the USB variant's price).
Cons: The TMC2240 sibling (SB2240) costs more for the same board, but the premium varies widely by retailer (about 30% more at Kamami, only ~$4 more at BIQU); USB-C is mainly for flashing, not a substitute for CAN in normal use; An RP2040 variant of the SB2209 CAN is now sold alongside the STM32 version, so listings need care; TMC2209 has less diagnostic headroom than the TMC2240
Pros: Purpose-built drop-in fit for the Voron StealthBurner; Onboard ADXL345 accelerometer for Klipper input shaping; MAX31865 supports PT100/PT1000 sensing up to 500C; CAN bus replaces the whole toolhead wiring bundle with one XT30 cable; Independent fan voltage selection (5V/12V/24V)

Name: Nitehawk 36
Description: The 36mm companion to the Nitehawk SB, sharing the same RP2040 MCU, USB-first approach, and LDO build quality. Where the Nitehawk SB targets Stealthburner specifically, the Nitehawk 36 fits the broader 36mm toolboard mount ecosystem. Ideal for non-SB toolhead designs that accept 36mm boards when you want to avoid CAN bus infrastructure. All the same trade-offs as the Nitehawk SB apply — simplicity and quality at a premium, with less community documentation than the EBB36 path.
Cons:
- USB only: same interface limitation as Nitehawk SB
- Fewer purpose-built toolhead mounts than SB variant
- Higher price than CAN alternatives at equivalent specs
- 36mm community toolhead ecosystem smaller than Stealthburner ecosystem
Pros:
- Same USB-first philosophy as Nitehawk SB: no CAN infrastructure needed
- 36mm form factor accommodates toolheads where Stealthburner won't fit
- RP2040 dual-core 133MHz with ADXL345 onboard
- Neopixel outputs, dual fans
- LDO build quality throughout

Name: EBB SB2240
Description: BigTreeTech's CAN toolhead board designed as a drop-in fit for the Voron StealthBurner, the TMC2240 variant of the EBB SB2209. It combines an STM32G0B1 MCU, an onboard TMC2240 extruder driver in SPI mode, an ADXL345 accelerometer for input shaping, and a MAX31865 for PT100/PT1000 sensing, all connected over CAN bus or USB-C. A single XT30 cable carries power and CAN data, replacing the usual bundle of toolhead wires. Price basis: $59.99 at BIQU (the manufacturer's store; sold out there — Kamami lists it at zł184.84, about $46.42, in stock).
Cons: Costs more than the SB2209 sibling for the same board, but the premium varies widely by retailer (about 30% more at Kamami, only ~$4 more at BIQU); USB-C is mainly for flashing, not a substitute for CAN in normal use; TMC2240's SPI mode needs a different Klipper config than the SB2209's UART mode
Pros: Purpose-built drop-in fit for the Voron StealthBurner; Onboard ADXL345 accelerometer for Klipper input shaping; MAX31865 supports PT100/PT1000 sensing up to 500C; CAN bus replaces the whole toolhead wiring bundle with one XT30 cable; Independent fan voltage selection (5V/12V/24V); TMC2240 in SPI mode gives wider diagnostics and more headroom than the SB2209's TMC2209

Name: Klipper ToolBoard for Roto Extruder
Description: The Klipper ToolBoard for Roto Extruder is E3D's Klipper-native toolboard for the Revo Roto, designed by Robert Lorincz of Orbiter Projects. It mounts directly to the Roto and talks to the Raspberry Pi over protected automotive-grade USB, with a TMC2209 extruder driver, an STM32F042 MCU and an onboard LIS2DW12 accelerometer for input shaping. It drives one 24 V part-cooling fan and one 5 V heatsink fan, and accepts NTC or PT1000 sensors for standard and high-temperature Revo HeaterCores up to 500 C.
Verdict Label: Plug-and-play Klipper board for the Revo Roto
Cons:
USB-only - no CAN option, so it needs a USB run back to the host
Sold out at E3D at time of check, though Filastruder had it in stock
Does not include the Roto extruder itself
Pros:
Mounts directly to the Roto with automotive-grade USB to the Pi - no CAN adapter needed
Onboard LIS2DW12 accelerometer for Klipper input shaping
Accepts both NTC and PT1000 sensors, so standard and high-temperature Revo HeaterCores both work
Fused USB adaptor board protects the Pi's USB port

Name: U2C v2.1
Description: The BTT U2C is not a toolboard — it's a USB-to-CAN bridge adapter. It connects to the Pi/host via USB and provides a CAN bus port for toolboards like the EBB36. If your mainboard lacks a native CAN transceiver (SKR 3 EZ, older Octopus v1.0, Fysetc S6), the U2C is the standard way to add CAN capability. If you're running an Octopus Pro v1.1, Manta M8P v2, or Leviathan, you don't need one — those boards have native CAN. Included here for context as a common companion to toolboards in Voron CAN builds.
Compatible Toolheads: N/A — bridge device, not a toolboard
Cons:
- Not a toolboard — provides zero extruder, hotend, or fan control
- Mainboards with native CAN (Octopus Pro v1.1, Manta M8P v2, Leviathan) don't need this
- Adds a USB device to manage and an extra cable to route
- Known RF interference issues with BTT Pi or Manta CB1 near Beacon probes — inline USB hub required as workaround
Pros:
- Enables full CAN bus toolboard setup on any mainboard with a free USB port
- Small and inexpensive (~$8) — lowest cost path to CAN bus
- Plug-and-play with EBB36 and most BTT toolboards
- Supported by Klipper's USB-CAN bridge mode

Name: SHT36 V3
Description: CAN/RS232 toolboard for 3D printer extruder heads (36mm / NEMA14/17 motors) with onboard TMC2209, LIS2DW accelerometer and two controllable fans; the Max version adds an LDC1612 eddy-current chip for bed-mesh probing and works with both Klipper and RRF.
Verdict Label: Strong EBB36 alternative — RP2040, LIS2DW, and an eddy-probe option
Cons:
Many variants (V3 / Plus / Eddy / Max) — easy to buy the wrong one
Board-only price varies by variant and is hard to pin down
RS232 mode needs a separate UTOR adapter
Mellow documentation is primarily in Chinese
Pros:
RP2040 133MHz dual-core MCU with CAN FD support
Onboard TMC2209 stepper driver
LIS2DW accelerometer for Klipper input shaping
Two controllable fan outputs
CAN + RS232 + USB connectivity, Klipper and RRF support
Max variant adds an LDC1612 eddy-current probe for bed-mesh scanning

Name: Tool Board 1LC
Description: The Duet 3 Tool Board 1LC is Duet3D's CAN-FD expansion board for direct-drive extruders, built around a 48 MHz ATSAMC21G18A MCU with a TMC2209 stepper driver. It puts the extruder motor, heater, temperature sensors, two fans, filament monitor and Z probe on the tool itself, leaving only CAN-FD and power wires to run back to the Duet 3 mainboard or Tool Distribution Board. Its mounting holes and connector layout match the E3D Hemera XS (v1.3), and v1.1 and later boards add an LIS3DH accelerometer for input shaping under RepRapFirmware; it can also run Klipper.
Cons:
12-32 V input and a 5 A heater output cap it at 120 W at 24 V - modest next to newer TMC2240 boards
Needs a Duet 3 mainboard or Tool Distribution Board for CAN-FD - not a standalone Klipper USB board
Mounting pattern is Hemera/Hemera XS, so other extruders need a bracket
Pros:
The original Duet CAN-FD toolboard - mature, open-hardware, and backed by full Duet documentation
Onboard LIS3DH accelerometer (v1.1+) for RRF input shaping
Two thermistor/PT1000 inputs plus filament monitor and Z-probe connectors cover a full direct-drive tool
Also runs Klipper (sample config in the Klipper repo)

Name: Orbitool O2S
Description: A USB toolboard for the Orbiter v2 / v2.5 extruder with STM32F072 MCU, TMC2240 driver, onboard ADXL345 accelerometer and part + hotend fan outputs, communicating with the host over USB.
Verdict Label: USB toolboard purpose-built for the Orbiter extruder
Cons:
Orbiter-only — not a general-purpose toolboard
USB-only, no CAN option
List price ($91.80) is steep; the $50.49 street price is a flash sale
Hotend connector type is undocumented
Pros:
Onboard TMC2240 stepper driver
ADXL345 accelerometer for Klipper input shaping
Purpose-built for the Orbiter v2 / v2.5 extruder
USB connection — no CAN bus infrastructure needed
Two fan outputs (part + hotend)

Name: SHT36 v2
Description: Mellow's toolboard answer to the BTT EBB36, using the same STM32G0B1CBT6 chip with FDCAN bus support. Hardware specs are essentially equivalent: TMC2209, ADXL345, Neopixel, USB-C fallback. The SHT36 v2 integrates well with the broader Mellow/Fly ecosystem (Fly-Super8, FLY-Gemini, etc.). A solid option if you're already using Mellow mainboards and want a consistent vendor stack, or if EBB36 stock is constrained.
Cons:
- Fewer Voron-specific guides than EBB36
- Mellow documentation is primarily in Chinese — English translations available but sometimes lag
- Community config files less widely shared than BTT equivalents
Pros:
- Same STM32G0B1CBT6 MCU as EBB36 v1.2 — identical CAN and Klipper support
- USB-C fallback for flashing
- ADXL345 and Neopixel onboard
- Active Mellow ecosystem and Fly-OS integration

Name: GBB15
Description: An open-source gantry-mounted CAN stepper driver board by skuep for 15mm aluminium extrusions, aimed mainly at PrintersForAnts printers such as the Micron. It puts two TMC2209 drivers for the A/B gantry motors directly on the gantry, so only CAN and power need routing to the frame, and it can also serve as a USB-to-CAN bridge for a Voron 0 or Trident. It has no hotend heater or fan outputs — it is a gantry driver board, not a toolhead board — and is sold assembled by Fabreeko and West3D.
Verdict Label: Niche gantry A/B driver for PrintersForAnts builds
Cons:
No hotend heater or fan outputs — gantry motors only, not a toolhead board
DIY heritage: work-in-progress repo; self-build needs JLCPCB assembly plus hand-soldered parts and a thermal pad to the extrusion
Must remove the 120R CAN termination resistor to run an umbilical to a CAN toolhead
Niche fit: designed for 15mm extrusions / PrintersForAnts Micron builds
Pros:
Two TMC2209 drivers on the gantry cut umbilical wiring to just CAN + power
Doubles as a USB-to-CAN bridge for Voron 0 / Trident
Open-source design with full KiCad, BOM and Klipper config on GitHub
Sold assembled by Fabreeko and West3D at $39.99 — no JLCPCB order needed

Name: Xol Toolhead Board
Description: The Xol Toolhead Board by ruiqimao is a passive wiring breakout PCB made for Armchair Engineering's Xol toolhead. It consolidates the toolhead wiring onto one board: one hotend cooling fan and two part-cooling fan JST-XH connectors, a Micro-Fit heater connector, a Micro-Fit thermistor connector, a Neopixel JST-XH connector, two auxiliary JST-XH connectors and the extruder motor connector, with selectable fan voltage (5V, Alt, 24V) and an integrated carriage-screw mount. It has no MCU, stepper driver or communications bus - it only tidies the wiring back to the mainboard.
Cons:
Passive breakout only - no MCU, driver or CAN/USB, so all wiring still runs back to the mainboard
Fits the Armchair Engineering Xol toolhead only
Fan and heater connections are JST-XH/Micro-Fit, so the harness needs the right crimps
Pros:
Covers every Xol connection - heater, thermistor, extruder motor, 3 fans, Neopixel and 2 aux - on one tidy PCB
Selectable fan voltage (5V, Alt, 24V) suits different fan builds
In stock at Fabreeko with a 5.0/5 rating, and a share of sales goes to the designer

Name: SB2040 V3 Pro
Description: Mellow's Stealthburner-specific toolboard built around the RP2040 dual-core MCU rather than the STM32 used by EBB36. The RP2040's ADC is notably faster than the STM32G0B1's, which is a tangible benefit for ADXL345 resonance testing accuracy. Supports CAN bus primary with USB-C fallback, onboard TMC2209, and Neopixel outputs. The main argument against it: the EBB36 has a larger config library and more Voron community familiarity, which matters when something goes wrong at midnight.
Cons:
- RP2040 CAN support in Klipper historically less mature than STM32 — mostly resolved now but community muscle memory favors EBB
- Smaller community than EBB36: fewer configs, fewer documented build logs
- Fysetc support and documentation quality is variable
Pros:
- RP2040 dual-core 133MHz — faster ADC sampling benefits ADXL345 resonance testing
- Designed specifically for Stealthburner geometry: clean integration
- CAN bus + USB-C fallback
- ADXL345 and Neopixel support onboard

Name: ToolBoard for Roto Extruder
Description: This is the Duet 3 Roto Toolboard, Duet3D's CAN-FD toolboard for the E3D Revo Roto extruder, sold by E3D. It pairs a 120 MHz ATSAME51G19A MCU with a TMC2240 extruder driver and connects the Roto motor, Revo heater and thermistor, heatsink fan and secondary temperature sensor using the E3D supplied connectors. It adds an integrated LIS2DW accelerometer and an LDC1612 inductive sensor for the Duet scanning Z probe, two PWM fan outputs, and four IO ports for endstops, filament monitoring and Z probing, leaving only power and a CAN-FD twisted pair to run back to the mainboard.
Verdict Label: The RRF-native Roto toolboard, with scanning Z probe built in
Cons:
RepRapFirmware only in practice - no Klipper sample config exists for it (E3D makes a separate Klipper Roto board)
Roto motor must stay under 600 mA, so the driver's extra current is mostly unused
Sold out at E3D at time of check, though Filastruder had it in stock
Pros:
Purpose-built for the Revo Roto, with the Duet scanning Z probe coil built in (Filastruder includes 2 coils)
TMC2240 driver and 120 MHz SAME51 give it headroom over the Klipper Roto board
Takes the Roto's E3D connectors plug-and-play, plus 4 IO ports and a Neopixel header
Integrated LIS2DW accelerometer and LDC1612 inductive sensor for scanning Z probe

Name: Nitehawk SB V2
Description: LDO Stealthburner toolboard, V2.0. A USB toolhead PCB with an STM32G0B1 MCU, TMC2209 stepper driver, and ADXL345 accelerometer integrated into one board. The V2 redesign swaps the RP2040 for the STM32G0B1, adds a USB hub with a secondary USB port and a general-purpose I2C port, keys the fan-adapter headers to prevent misalignment, and moves the probe, TH0 and XY endstop ports to JST-PH2.0. You route a standard USB cable to the toolhead, bypassing CAN bus entirely.
Cons:
- USB only: some builders prefer CAN for cleaner toolhead wiring
- Higher price than EBB36 (~$35 vs ~$15)
- USB is not a "fallback" here — it's the only interface; no CAN option if you later want it
- CAN remains de facto Voron community recommendation; Nitehawk adoption is growing but EBB configs are more plentiful
Pros:
- USB-only: eliminates CAN bus infrastructure entirely — no U2C, no CAN wiring, no CANFD config headaches
- Runs over existing USB cable — simpler toolhead wiring than CAN at longer toolhead distances
- RP2040 dual-core MCU with fast ADXL345 sampling
- LDO build quality: notably better component selection and QC than BTT AliExpress stock
- ADXL345, Neopixel, dual fans in a purpose-built Stealthburner form factor

Name: H36 Combo V1.3
Description: FYSETC's high-temperature CAN/USB toolboard built around the STM32G0B1T3, rated to 125C in CAN mode with the ADXL345-EP accelerometer option. It carries an onboard TMC2209 driver, a USB 2.0 hub with two spare ports for probes or cameras, four fan outputs, and a 5A HE0 heater output, connected via an XT30 umbilical with a custom cable included. Aimed at enclosed, high-chamber-temperature Voron toolheads where a standard toolboard would overheat.
Verdict Label: High-temp CAN/USB toolboard with built-in USB hub
Cons:
125C operation is CAN-only; the USB hub chip is not 125C rated
V1.2/V1.3 silkscreen errors on the XT30 connector and HE0 markings (documented; bottom silkscreen is correct)
Pricier than EBB36/SHT36 for the same basic job
FYSETC docs mix V1/V2 variants, so check you are on the V1.3 page
Pros:
125C-rated MCU with ADXL345-EP option for high-temperature chambers (CAN mode)
Onboard USB 2.0 hub gives two spare USB ports for probes or cameras
Onboard TMC2209 and ADXL345 input shaping
Four fan outputs with tach feedback
CAN/USB switchable; XT30 umbilical with custom cable included

Name: EBB36 CAN v1.2
Description: The de facto standard Voron toolboard. EBB36 CAN v1.2 uses the STM32G0B1CBT6 with FDCAN support, giving it better CAN bus performance than the older F0-based v1.0. The v1.2 revision fixes a DFU mode issue that inadvertently powered the hotend during firmware flashing. Combines TMC2209 extruder driver, ADXL345 for resonance compensation, USB-C fallback, and dual fan outputs in a 36mm package. The community has built out a comprehensive config and mount ecosystem around this board — if you're building a Voron and don't have a strong reason to use something else, this is the pick.
Cons:
- Requires CAN bus infrastructure: mainboard with native CAN or a BTT U2C bridge
- Initial CAN setup has steeper learning curve than USB toolboards
- BTT has documented RF interference issues with their Pi/CB1 boards near Beacon probes
Pros:
- STM32G0B1 with FDCAN — best CAN implementation for toolboards
- ADXL345 onboard for resonance tuning via Klipper
- USB fallback for flashing and debugging without full CAN setup
- Massive community support: guides, configs, mounts for every Voron variant
- v1.2 fixes DFU mode heating bug (hotend IO moved PA2→PB13)

Name: Huvud
Description: The original community-designed CAN toolboard, created by Pontus Borg (bananas-blender) and a key reason CAN toolboards became mainstream in the Voron community. Runs on the STM32F103C8T6 — the same 'blue pill' chip used in early reprap boards. CAN-only with no USB fallback, and lacks an onboard ADXL345. Both are significant omissions by current standards. Still operational and supported by Klipper, but the EBB36 v1.2 and Nitehawk boards have made it obsolete for new builds. If you have one running, keep it — don't spec it for new builds.
Cons:
- No ADXL345 onboard — resonance tuning requires external probe or skipping
- CAN only: no USB fallback makes initial flashing and debugging significantly harder
- STM32F103C8T6 is older and slower (72MHz) with limited flash
- Community has moved on: EBB36 and Nitehawk offer more features at similar or lower cost
- Design is effectively frozen — no active development
Pros:
- Pioneered the CAN toolboard concept for prosumer FDM — historically significant
- Open source design: PCB files, BOM, and documentation on GitHub
- Compact form factor
- Proven CAN bus reliability in early Voron community builds

Name: EBB42 CAN v1.1
Description: The larger sibling of the EBB36, sharing identical MCU, driver, and peripheral specs in a 42mm form factor. Runs the same STM32G0B1CBT6 with FDCAN bus support. The 42mm footprint fits some toolhead designs that can't accommodate 36mm boards, and some builders prefer the slightly larger PCB for connector access. If you're building a Stealthburner, the EBB36 has more mount options — EBB42 is worth considering for custom or 42mm-native toolhead designs.
Cons:
- 42mm format has fewer pre-designed Stealthburner/Clockwork 2 mounts than EBB36
- Same CAN infrastructure requirements as EBB36
- Less community documentation compared to the 36mm variant
- Choose EBB36 unless you specifically need 42mm PCB footprint
Pros:
- Identical electronics to EBB36 v1.2: same STM32G0B1CBT6 MCU, TMC2209, ADXL345
- 42mm format fits some toolheads better — particularly on non-SB designs
- USB-C fallback for flashing
- FDCAN bus for reliable high-speed CAN communication
